Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: We examined the dimensionality of four cognitive-linguistic skills (phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge) among Chinese-English bilingual children (N = 1295, M age = 8.61, SD = 1.46).
We tested five theoretically motivated models within each language and proficiency group (emerging vs. advanced bilinguals) to examine the measurement structure of these skills.
Results revealed a common three-factor solution (phonological, orthographic, and morpho-lexical dimensions) in L1 Chinese across proficiency levels.

In L2 English, a phonological-morphological dimension emerged for emerging bilinguals, while a morpho-lexical dimension emerged for advanced bilinguals, with an orthographic awareness dimension for both groups.

Across both languages, morphological awareness and vocabulary consistently clustered into a shared morpho-lexical dimension in advanced bilinguals, reflecting increasing integration of cognitive-linguistic processes.

These findings highlight the dynamic nature of bilingual literacy development and provide a developmental framework for understanding how cognitive-linguistic skills become increasingly coordinated across languages.

Bilingual individuals engage in a dynamic process of simultaneously developing cognitive-linguistic skills related to phonology, orthography, and semantics, across languages throughout their lives (Grosjean, 2010).
text.formatted: Bilingual individuals engage in a dynamic process of simultaneously developing cognitive-linguistic skills related to phonology, orthography, and semantics, across languages throughout their lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Grosjean, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These skills are thought to underlie bilingual literacy development, yet their dimensionality remains uncertain.

While studies have investigated the impacts of cognitive-linguistic skills on bilingual literacy (e.g., Deacon et al., 2009; McBride-Chang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Yeong & Rickard Liow, 2011), limited studies have thoroughly and systematically examined the dimensionality of these skills.
text.formatted: While studies have investigated the impacts of cognitive-linguistic skills on bilingual literacy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Deacon et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">McBride-Chang et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wang et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Yeong & Rickard Liow, 2011)</ref>, limited studies have thoroughly and systematically examined the dimensionality of these skills.

text.text: Additionally, the relationship among cognitive-linguistic skills may be developmentally dynamic and may vary with language proficiency (Deacon et al., 2009; Perfetti & Hart, 2002; Tomblin & Zhang, 2006; Tong et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Additionally, the relationship among cognitive-linguistic skills may be developmentally dynamic and may vary with language proficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Deacon et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Perfetti & Hart, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Tomblin & Zhang, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Tong et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: However, few studies, to our knowledge, have adopted a developmental perspective to understand how these skills evolve as children develop bilingual language and literacy.
To address this gap, in the present study we examined the developmental dimensionality of cognitive-linguistic skills in Chinese-English bilingual children with varying proficiency levels.

Reading is a complex process that relies on multiple cognitive-linguistic skills operating at different aspects, such as phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge (e.g., Landerl et al., 2022; McBride et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Reading is a complex process that relies on multiple cognitive-linguistic skills operating at different aspects, such as phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Landerl et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">McBride et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies have provided considerable insights into how these cognitivelinguistic skills contribute to reading ability in both Chinese and English (e.g., McBride-Chang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Yeong & Rickard Liow, 2011).
text.formatted: Previous studies have provided considerable insights into how these cognitivelinguistic skills contribute to reading ability in both Chinese and English (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">McBride-Chang et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wang et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Yeong & Rickard Liow, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Although these studies have established the importance of each of these skills in bilingual literacy, fewer have investigated their interrelationships, namely, whether they reflect distinct dimensions or a DIMENSIONALITY OF BILINGUAL SKILLS smaller number of unified underlying constructs.

Indeed, the few studies that have explored this question (e.g., Keenan et al., 2008; Lonigan & Burgess, 2017; Tomblin & Zhang, 2006) have primarily focused on the structure of reading skills per se rather than on their underlying cognitive-linguistic skills.
text.formatted: Indeed, the few studies that have explored this question (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Keenan et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Lonigan & Burgess, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Tomblin & Zhang, 2006)</ref> have primarily focused on the structure of reading skills per se rather than on their underlying cognitive-linguistic skills.

text.text: While such research has advanced our understanding of reading skills as a multidimensional construct, it is equally important to investigate the dimensionality (underlying structure and interrelations) of the foundational cognitivelinguistic constructs.
A clearer understanding of these skills is crucial to inform early, detailed assessment and intervention for bilingual children at risk of language and literacy difficulties (Huo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A clearer understanding of these skills is crucial to inform early, detailed assessment and intervention for bilingual children at risk of language and literacy difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Huo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Developmental research has long suggested that the latent organization of cognitivelinguistic skills may change over development, although existing findings have been mixed.

Some studies have reported developmental reorganization of cognitive-linguistic skills (e.g., Tong & McBride-Chang, 2010), whereas others have found relatively stable latent structures despite age-related improvements in performance (e.g., Lonigan et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Some studies have reported developmental reorganization of cognitive-linguistic skills (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Tong & McBride-Chang, 2010)</ref>, whereas others have found relatively stable latent structures despite age-related improvements in performance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lonigan et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Tong and McBride-Chang (2010) showed that the structure of phonological, morphological, orthographic, and sub-character processing in Chinese children underwent dynamic reorganization rather than simple age-related differentiation.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Tong and McBride-Chang (2010)</ref> showed that the structure of phonological, morphological, orthographic, and sub-character processing in Chinese children underwent dynamic reorganization rather than simple age-related differentiation.

text.text: They identified a print-nonprint distinction in kindergarten, a fully differentiated four-factor structure in Grade 2, and a more integrated configuration by Grade 5, in which morphological and orthographic skills clustered into a broad lexical-morpho-orthographic factor alongside a distinct phonological factor.

This developmental pattern suggests a progression from coarse print sensitivity to increasingly differentiated metalinguistic skills, followed by higher-order integration of meaning-related processes.

In contrast, in a study with English-speaking preschool children, Lonigan et al. (2009) reported that phonological awareness, memory, and lexical access formed distinct latent factors that remained largely invariant across the preschool years.
text.formatted: In contrast, in a study with English-speaking preschool children, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lonigan et al. (2009)</ref> reported that phonological awareness, memory, and lexical access formed distinct latent factors that remained largely invariant across the preschool years.

text.text: Although children's performance on these cognitive-linguistic skills improved substantially with age, their underlying latent organization remained largely stable.

It should be noted, however, that previous studies examining the dimensionality of reading and related skills have focused on monolingual children (Lonigan et al., 2009; Lonigan & Burgess, 2017; Tomblin & Zhang, 2006).
text.formatted: It should be noted, however, that previous studies examining the dimensionality of reading and related skills have focused on monolingual children <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lonigan et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Lonigan & Burgess, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Tomblin & Zhang, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Although a few studies have examined bilingual populations (e.g., Sun et al., 2018), they have primarily focused on cross-language structural correspondence rather than developmental changes in dimensionality across different stages of bilingual proficiency.
text.formatted: Although a few studies have examined bilingual populations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sun et al., 2018)</ref>, they have primarily focused on cross-language structural correspondence rather than developmental changes in dimensionality across different stages of bilingual proficiency.

text.text: This gap leaves an important question unanswered: Whether phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge show greater differentiation or integration at different levels of bilingual proficiency, and whether their organization differs between children's first (L1) and second (L2) languages.

The present study aimed to address this question by examining how these cognitive-linguistic skills are organized across proficiency groups in both the L1 and L2 of Chinese-English bilingual children in Hong Kong.

To guide our modeling approach, we drew on theoretical accounts and empirical evidence that suggest how particular cognitive-linguistic skill domains cluster or diverge over the course of development (e.g., Deacon & Kirby, 2004; McBride-Chang et al., 2008).

text.text: We discuss each dimension separately below.
Orthographic and phonological processing skills are often theorized to function as a distinct but intertwined mechanism.

Within dual-route models of reading, word identification is proposed to rely on coordinated mappings between orthographic representations and their corresponding phonological codes (e.g., Grainger & Ziegler, 2011).

text.text: In English, longitudinal studies have shown reciprocal relations between phonological sensitivity and letter-sound knowledge, suggesting interdependent development of the two systems (Burgess & Lonigan, 1998; Castles & Coltheart, 2004).

text.text: Previous findings further indicate that orthographic information can influence performance even in tasks primarily targeting phonological processing (Rastle & Brysbaert, 2006).

text.text: Similar mechanisms have also been proposed for Chinese.

Chinese is a morphosyllabic writing system in which phonological information is often embedded within orthographic structures, particularly through phonetic radicals (Perfetti et al., 2005; Tong & McBride-Chang, 2010; Zhou & Marslen-Wilson, 2000).

text.text: These findings suggest a unified dimension capturing children's sensitivity to the phonological-morphological (sound-meaning) structure of English words.
In turn, Chinese is a morphosyllabic language in which syllables and morphemes are tightly aligned, with each typically encoded by a single written character.

This structural correspondence means that phonological representations are closely connected with morphemic information, allowing early phonological (syllabic) sensitivity to support the development of morphological analysis (Pan et al., 2016).

text.text: However, because Chinese contains a large number of homophones (e.g., 梨/li2/ 'pear' and 离/li2/ 'to leave,' or 鞋/xie2/ 'shoe' and 邪/xie2/ 'evil'), phonological information alone is often insufficient to distinguish lexical meanings, requiring children to integrate phonological and morphological cues during word recognition.

Consistent with this interaction, empirical studies have shown that phonological and morphological awareness are highly correlated in Chinese children and jointly contribute to literacy development (e.g., Tong & McBride-Chang, 2010).

text.text: A third theoretical account emphasizes the interdependence between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge.

Morphological awareness plays an increasingly central role in reading development across languages and writing systems, making its link with vocabulary progressively stronger as semantic demands rise (Deacon et al., 2014; Kieffer & Lesaux, 2012; McBride-Chang et al., 2008; Spencer et al., 2015).

text.text: Morphological analysis also provides a powerful generative mechanism for vocabulary expansion by allowing learners to infer meanings from internal word structure (Crosson et al., 2021; Levesque et al., 2017).

text.text: Another important theoretical question in bilingual literacy development concerns whether the dimensionality of cognitive-linguistic skills varies with language proficiency.

The Lexical Constituency Model (Perfetti et al., 2005) proposes that skilled reading relies on coordinated orthographic, phonological, and semantic constituents that remain functionally distinguishable despite their interaction during word recognition.
text.formatted: The Lexical Constituency Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Perfetti et al., 2005)</ref> proposes that skilled reading relies on coordinated orthographic, phonological, and semantic constituents that remain functionally distinguishable despite their interaction during word recognition.

text.text: Consistent with this view, dimensionality studies have identified phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge as separable constructs in early literacy development (e.g., Sun et al., 2018; Tong & McBride-Chang, 2010).

text.text: These findings suggest that cognitive-linguistic skills may initially emerge as distinct and functionally separable components.
An alternative perspective emphasizes increasing integration among cognitivelinguistic representations with literacy development.

According to interactive models of reading development, such as the triangle model of reading (Harm & Seidenberg, 2004), orthographic, phonological, and semantic representations are acquired through interconnected learning mechanisms and become increasingly coordinated with experience.

text.text: Consistent with this perspective, Tong and McBride-Chang (2010) provided evidence that cognitive-linguistic skills that were initially distinguishable became increasingly interconnected over the course of Chinese literacy development.

text.text: Similarly, the Lexical Quality Hypothesis (Perfetti & Hart, 2002) argues that skilled reading relies on tightly bound lexical representations in which orthographic, phonological, and semantic information is simultaneously activated.

text.text: From this perspective, developmental changes in the dimensionality of cognitive-linguistic skills may reflect increasing coordination among initially distinct components, resulting in greater overlap among latent constructs as language and literacy proficiency increases.

Building on theoretical and empirical evidence regarding the interdependence of cognitive-linguistic skills, the present study investigated how the dimensionality of four cognitive-linguistic abilities (i.e., phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge) is organized across development in Chinese-English bilingual children.

The study further examined whether the latent factor structure of these skills is similar or different across bilingual proficiency levels, and whether the structural organization differs across the two languages.
We systematically tested and compared a set of theoretically motivated factor structures for cognitive-linguistic skills for each language and proficiency group (Figure 1).

text.text: In doing so, we sought to characterize the dimensionality of cognitive-linguistic skills in bilingual learners of L1 Chinese and L2 English.

By mapping how these skill structures evolve both within and across languages, we sought to provide a developmental framework for understanding how bilingual children progressively coordinate phonological, orthographic, morphological, and lexical processing as their bilingual proficiency grows.

Based on the theory and literature reviewed above, we hypothesized that the dimensionality of cognitive-linguistic skills would differ across L1 Chinese and L2 English, given their different developmental and linguistic contexts (Cheng et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2023).

text.text: All participants were L1 Cantonese-speaking children recruited from local primary schools in Hong Kong (N = 1295, M age = 8.61, SD = 1.46).
They were recruited from schools across different districts to make the sample as demographically representative as possible.
The sample consisted of two proficiency groups: emerging bilinguals (N = 593, M age = 7.37, SD = 0.74) and advanced bilinguals (N = 702, M age = 9.63, SD = 0.98).
The emerging bilingual group comprised children in Grades 1-2, whereas the advanced bilingual group comprised children in Grades 3-5.

This grade-based grouping was intended to capture differences in children's bilingual language and literacy proficiency in both Chinese and English based on the local educational setting: Hong Kong children typically speak Cantonese Chinese as their first and primary language and begin learning English as a second language as early as kindergarten (age 3) and are therefore considered sequential bilinguals (Hong Kong Education Bureau, 2017).

text.text: The syllable deletion task consisted of 29 test items.
Children were asked to say a word/non-word without saying one of its syllables (e.g., /jyun4 zi2 bat1/ 'pen' without /zi2/).
A child's score was the total number correct (max = 29), with Cronbach's alpha reliability of .82.
The onset deletion task consisted of 22 test items.
Children were asked to say a single-or two-syllable word without the initial phoneme of the word (e.g., say /si1/ without /s/ or /hun2 kwat1/ without /h/).
A child's score was the total number correct (max = 22), with Cronbach's alpha reliability of .98.

English phonological awareness was assessed using an invented spelling task (McBride-Chang, 1998), which required children to analyze spoken pseudowords and represent their sound structures in writing.

text.text: The task consisted of 12 single-syllable pseudowords ranging from three to six letters in length.
Children listened to a recording of a native English speaker pronouncing each pseudoword and were instructed to spell the word on a response sheet.
Responses were scored using a 5-point scale (0-5), with higher scores reflecting more accurate phonological representations in spelling.
A child's score was the sum of the item scores (max = 60), with Cronbach's alpha reliability of .93.
Chinese morphological awareness was assessed using a morphological compounding task (McBride-Chang et al., 2003) and a morpho-syntax task (Chik et al., 2012).

text.text: In the morphological compounding task, children were orally presented with short scenarios (e.g., "We call paper that is white in color white paper") and then were asked to come up with a compound word based on a new related example (e.g., "So what do we call paper if it is red?"
; correct answer: "red paper").
Items were ordered by grade level, and the section was DIMENSIONALITY OF BILINGUAL SKILLS discontinued after three consecutive incorrect responses.
One point was awarded for each correct response (max = 44).
Cronbach's alpha reliability was .90.
In the morpho-syntax task, children were presented with a written sentence while simultaneously hearing it read aloud.

For each item, they were asked to identify the incorrect word and replace it with a more appropriate one (e.g., 科學家經常有新的發覺 "Scientists always have new awareness", in which the incorrect word 發覺 'awareness' should be replaced with 發現 'discovery').
The task consisted of 18 test items.

Each item was worth up to three points: one point for correctly identifying the error and two points for accurately replacing it (one point for syntactic appropriateness and one point for semantic appropriateness; partially correct responses received 0.5 point where applicable).
A child's score was the sum of the item scores (max = 54).
Cronbach's alpha reliability was .91.
English morphological awareness was assessed using a morpheme compounding task (McBride-Chang et al., 2008) and a WUG test (Berko, 1958).
text.formatted: English morphological awareness was assessed using a morpheme compounding task <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(McBride-Chang et al., 2008)</ref> and a WUG test <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Berko, 1958)</ref>.

text.text: The morpheme compounding task consisted of 11 items.

Children were first presented with an example of how to construct a compound word (e.g., "a box we use to hold our lunch is called a lunchbox") and then were asked to come up with a compound word based on a new example (e.g., "What do we call a box that we use to hold dinner?").
Each correct answer was given 1 point (max = 11), with Cronbach's alpha reliability of .83.
The WUG test consisted of four items.
The first two items asked children to make nouns plural, and the other two asked them to form a progressive and a past tense, respectively.
Two points were given for the correct answer, and 1 point was given for the partially correct answer (max = 8).
Cronbach's alpha reliability was .90.
Chinese orthographic awareness was assessed using a lexical decision task (Ho et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Chinese orthographic awareness was assessed using a lexical decision task <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ho et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: A total of 60 characters were included, with 30 low-frequency Chinese characters and 30 pseudo-characters.

The pseudo-characters included two types of orthographic violations: 1) illegitimate combinations where semantic and phonetic radicals were positioned in nonstandard locations contrary to Chinese orthographic rules; 2) structurally impossible configurations formed by pairing two semantic radicals or two phonetic components.
Children were asked to distinguish between real and pseudo characters.
Each correctly identified item was given 1 point (max = 60), with Cronbach's alpha reliability of .93.
English orthographic awareness was assessed using a delayed copying task and a lexical decision task (Lo et al., 2018).

text.text: In the delayed copying task, children were required to copy an unfamiliar word after seeing it on a laptop screen.
The task consisted of 10 items with orthographically complex low-frequency words (6-11 letters; e.g., predicament, controversy).
Scoring followed Lo et al.'s (2018) procedure, and scores were allocated separately for copied letters and their positions.
text.formatted: Scoring followed <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lo et al.'s (2018)</ref> procedure, and scores were allocated separately for copied letters and their positions.

In the lexical decision task, children were required to distinguish an English nonword from three similar stimuli, including a real word (e.g., nice), a pseudoword (e.g., nise), and a nonword (e.g., niie).
The tasks consisted of 30 items, and one point was given for the correct identification (max = 30).
Cronbach's alpha reliability was .89.
Vocabulary knowledge in both Chinese and English was assessed using two tasks: expressive vocabulary and vocabulary definition.
The items were selected based on age of acquisition and arranged in increasing order of difficulty.
In Chinese, the expressive vocabulary and vocabulary definition tasks consisted of 23 and 27 items, respectively.
In the expressive vocabulary task, children were shown pictures of objects and situations and asked to name them in Cantonese.
The pictures were adapted from the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test-Third Edition (PPVT-III; Dunn & Dunn, 1997), and one point was awarded for each DIMENSIONALITY OF BILINGUAL SKILLS correct response.

text.text: In the vocabulary definition task, children were asked to define orally presented Chinese words.
Responses were scored from 0 to 2 according to the accuracy of the definitions.
The items were adapted from McBride-Chang et al. (2008).

Children completed the language and literacy assessment battery individually, supervised by trained research assistants with backgrounds in psychoeducational assessment who were fluent in Cantonese and English.
The tasks were administered in a single session of approximately 40 minutes.
Most children were tested in a quiet room at their school during school hours, while some children were tested at home for logistical reasons.
Before each test, the children were given a detailed explanation of the procedure and their consent was obtained.

First, to examine the dimensional structure of cognitive-linguistic skills across bilingual development, a series of confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) were conducted separately for emerging and advanced bilingual groups in each language.

Five theory-driven models (see Figure 1) were specified: (1) a one-factor model representing a general cognitive-linguistic ability (baseline model); (2) a four-factor model representing DIMENSIONALITY OF BILINGUAL SKILLS phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge as correlated but separable cognitive-linguistic skills (Model 2); (3) three alternative three-factor models reflecting different theoretical perspectives: Model 3A (phonological, orthographic, and morpho-lexical factor), Model 3B (phonologicalmorphological factor, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge), and Model 3C (orthographic-phonological factor, morphological awareness, and vocabulary knowledge).

text.text: The purpose of this study was to examine the developmental dimensionality of four key cognitive-linguistic skills (phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and vocabulary knowledge) in Chinese-English bilingual children.

By testing theoretically motivated models across two proficiency levels (emerging vs. advanced bilinguals), we aimed to determine whether these skills function as distinct dimensions or integrate into more general constructs as language proficiency develops.
Our results first showed that the structural organization of these skills differed across languages:
In L1 Chinese, a common three-factor structure (phonological, orthographic, and morpholexical) emerged across proficiency groups.
In contrast, the three-factor structure of L2 English differed across proficiency groups.
Among emerging bilinguals, phonological and morphological awareness formed a common factor, whereas vocabulary knowledge and orthographic awareness remained distinct.

In contrast, among advanced bilinguals, morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge formed a common morpho-lexical DIMENSIONALITY OF BILINGUAL SKILLS factor, while phonological and orthographic awareness remained distinct.
Morpho-lexical integration was evident in both Chinese proficiency groups but only in the advanced English group.
Together, these findings contribute to our understanding of how the organization of cognitive-linguistic skills varies across languages and may differ over the course of bilingual development.

The results first showed that L1 Chinese demonstrated a common three-factor structure across proficiency levels, with morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge consistently forming a shared morpho-lexical factor.
This pattern is consistent with the linguistic characteristics of Chinese, in which morphemes serve as the fundamental units of both word formation and lexical meaning.
Because most Chinese words are compounds composed of meaningful morphemes, vocabulary acquisition often requires sensitivity to morphological structure.

Previous studies have similarly demonstrated close associations between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge in Chinese-speaking children (Liu & McBride-Chang, 2010; Lu et al., 2025; McBride-Chang et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Previous studies have similarly demonstrated close associations between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge in Chinese-speaking children <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Liu & McBride-Chang, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Lu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">McBride-Chang et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that morphological and lexical knowledge may be functionally intertwined from relatively early phases of Chinese literacy development.
Compared with L2 English, which showed different factor structures across proficiency groups, L1 Chinese exhibited a more stable organizational pattern across groups.
One possible explanation is that morpho-lexical integration may emerge earlier in Chinese due to the morphosyllabic nature of the writing system.

Because Chinese characters simultaneously encode morphemic and semantic information, and because compound formation is highly productive, children are exposed to systematic links between morphological structure and lexical meaning from the beginning of literacy acquisition (Kuo & Anderson, 2006; McBride-Chang et al., 2008).

text.text: Consistent with this view, longitudinal DIMENSIONALITY OF BILINGUAL SKILLS studies have shown that associations between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge are already evident in kindergarten and the early primary grades in Chinese (Cheng et al., 2015; McBride-Chang et al., 2008).

text.text: Thus, the stable morpho-lexical factor observed across proficiency levels may reflect the earlier integration of morphological and lexical knowledge in L1 Chinese.
In contrast, our results for L2 English revealed different latent structures of cognitivelinguistic skills across proficiency groups, a pattern consistent with possible developmental reorganization.

The clustering of phonological and morphological awareness among emerging bilinguals suggests that, in the early phases of L2 English development, morphological processing may be closely tied to phonological processing.

Although morphology encompasses semantic, phonological, and syntactic information (Mahony et al., 2000), less proficient bilingual learners may initially access morphological structure through phonological awareness.
text.formatted: Although morphology encompasses semantic, phonological, and syntactic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Mahony et al., 2000)</ref>, less proficient bilingual learners may initially access morphological structure through phonological awareness.

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with evidence showing strong associations between phonological awareness and morphological awareness among young monolingual English readers (e.g., Cunningham & Carroll, 2015; Inoue et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with evidence showing strong associations between phonological awareness and morphological awareness among young monolingual English readers (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cunningham & Carroll, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Inoue et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: At early phases of second language acquisition, limited lexical knowledge may constrain direct access to morphemic meaning, leading children to rely more heavily on phonological cues when identifying and manipulating morphological units.
Interestingly, among advanced bilinguals, morphological awareness was more closely aligned with vocabulary knowledge, forming a unified morpho-lexical factor.
This difference between proficiency groups may reflect changes in the functional role of morphology during literacy acquisition.
Whereas morphology appears closely tied to phonological processing in earlier phases of L2 English development, it may increasingly support lexical and semantic representations as proficiency grows.

Consistent with this interpretation, morphological awareness has been associated with multiple aspects of vocabulary knowledge, including vocabulary breadth and depth, in English literacy development in both monolingual and bilingual contexts (Kieffer & Lesaux, 2012; Sparks & Deacon, 2015).
text.formatted: Consistent with this interpretation, morphological awareness has been associated with multiple aspects of vocabulary knowledge, including vocabulary breadth and depth, in English literacy development in both monolingual and bilingual contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kieffer & Lesaux, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Sparks & Deacon, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Morphological knowledge enables learners to recognize meaningful constituents in words, infer the meanings of unfamiliar words, and establish connections among morphologically related words (Carlisle, 2000; Kuo & Anderson, 2006).
text.formatted: Morphological knowledge enables learners to recognize meaningful constituents in words, infer the meanings of unfamiliar words, and establish connections among morphologically related words <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Carlisle, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kuo & Anderson, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is also consistent with theories that conceptualize morphology as an integrative mechanism linking phonological, orthographic, and semantic representations (Kirby & Bowers, 2017; Levesque et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This interpretation is also consistent with theories that conceptualize morphology as an integrative mechanism linking phonological, orthographic, and semantic representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kirby & Bowers, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Levesque et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As bilingual learners accumulate lexical experience, morphology may increasingly support the organization of semantic and lexical knowledge, aligning more closely with vocabulary knowledge at more advanced levels of L2 English development.

Importantly, morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge converged into a shared dimension across both languages, particularly among advanced bilinguals, suggesting that the two constructs may become increasingly interconnected at the latent construct level as language and literacy proficiency develops.
The Lexical Quality Hypothesis (Perfetti & Hart, 2002) provides a principled account of this convergence.
text.formatted: The Lexical Quality Hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Perfetti & Hart, 2002)</ref> provides a principled account of this convergence.

text.text: Rather than reflecting two independent skills, the observed pattern suggests that morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge increasingly draw on a shared system of high-quality lexical representations.

As these representations become more precise and well specified, the connections between form and meaning may become more tightly integrated, reducing the functional separability of morphological awareness and semantic access.
From a processing perspective, this shift can be understood as a transition from relatively sequential to increasingly coordinated operations.
For less proficient learners, morphological decomposition and meaning retrieval may occur in a stepwise manner.

With increasing proficiency, however, these processes may become more coordinated, such that morphological structure and lexical meaning are increasingly integrated during word recognition (Liang & Chen, 2014; see also Perfetti & Hart, 2002, for a discussion of the shared representational system).
text.formatted: With increasing proficiency, however, these processes may become more coordinated, such that morphological structure and lexical meaning are increasingly integrated during word recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Liang & Chen, 2014</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Perfetti & Hart, 2002</ref>, for a discussion of the shared representational system).

text.text: This increasing coordination may render the two constructs more interdependent and, at the latent level, less distinguishable.
These findings suggest that morpho-lexical integration may represent a fundamental organizational principle of cognitive-linguistic development.
Beyond representational integration, this convergence can also be understood as reflecting a mutually reinforcing developmental process (Carlisle, 2000; Kuo & Anderson, 2006; Nagy et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Beyond representational integration, this convergence can also be understood as reflecting a mutually reinforcing developmental process <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Carlisle, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kuo & Anderson, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Nagy et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: As learners accumulate morphological knowledge, they acquire productive tools for inferring and retaining the meanings of unfamiliar words, while expanding vocabulary in turn enhances sensitivity to shared morphemic structure.

Longitudinal evidence supports this reciprocal relation, showing that morphological awareness predicts vocabulary growth even after controlling for phonological skills, and that vocabulary knowledge, in turn, facilitates the acquisition of new morphological patterns (Sparks & Deacon, 2015).

text.text: Evidence from meta-analyses further supports this developmental pattern, indicating that the association between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge strengthens with age and represents one of the most robust relations among cognitive-linguistic skills (Cheng et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2023).

text.text: This increasing association is consistent with the view that the two constructs become progressively more integrated over the course of literacy development.
This morpho-lexical integration pattern can be further understood in light of language-specific properties.

In Chinese, the close mapping between morphemes and characters, together with the high productivity of compounding, links morphological analysis closely to lexical learning from the early stages of literacy development (McBride-Chang et al., 2008).

text.text: In English, although morphological processing involves the decomposition of roots and affixes, it serves a similar function in supporting the inference and generalization of word meanings (Carlisle, 2000; Nagy et al., 2006).

text.text: Despite these differences in writing systems, both languages exhibit a shared functional linkage between morphological processing and vocabulary development.
Taken together, these findings support the view that morpho-lexical integration reflects a consistent and developmentally driven feature of cognitive-linguistic (re)organization across languages.

Although the present study focused on within-language dimensionality, the observed convergence between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge across L1 Chinese and L2 English may also have implications for cross-language transfer.

The Linguistic Interdependence Hypothesis and the Transfer Facilitation Model (Koda & Reddy, 2008) suggest that metalinguistic skills developed in one language can support literacy development in another through shared underlying processes.

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with evidence from Chinese-English bilinguals showing that Chinese morphological awareness predicts English morphological awareness beyond other cognitive-linguistic factors (Lu et al., 2025).

text.text: Similarly, sensitivity to morphemic structure acquired through the compound-rich Chinese writing system may facilitate the development of comparable morphological skills in English (Luo et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, sensitivity to morphemic structure acquired through the compound-rich Chinese writing system may facilitate the development of comparable morphological skills in English <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Luo et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sun et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Given the role of morphology in vocabulary learning, such transfer may contribute indirectly to the increasingly close association between morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge observed in more proficient bilinguals.
Nevertheless, the present study did not directly examine cross-language transfer.
Future research should investigate whether the morpholexical dimension identified in L2 English is influenced by earlier development of morphological and lexical skills in L1 Chinese.
Several limitations are worth mentioning.
First, the present study relied on crosssectional proficiency groupings, limiting conclusions about within-individual structural reorganization and cross-language transfer.

Although similar morpho-lexical organization was identified across L1 Chinese and L2 English, longitudinal studies are needed to examine how these structures change over time and whether earlier L1 Chinese morpho-lexical skills predict the development of the corresponding dimension in L2 English.

Second, given that radicals constitute a fundamental feature of the Chinese writing system (McBride, 2016), future models could incorporate more fine-grained subcomponents, such as semantic radical awareness, to further strengthen the construct validity of the morpho-lexical dimension in Chinese.
Third, some of our tasks showed relatively lower Cronbach's alpha reliability.

This may partly reflect the nature of the assessment battery, in which multiple complementary subtasks were originally designed to provide a comprehensive assessment of a broader cognitivelinguistic skill.

Future research should examine the reliability and validity of these measures using alternative approaches, such as composite scores across complementary sub-tasks or higher-order latent-variable models that account for measurement error.
Fourth, in the CFA analysis, model selection was based on a balance between statistical fit and parsimony, particularly in cases where competing models showed highly similar fit indices.
Under such conditions, the selection of more parsimonious models may obscure subtle distinctions among latent constructs.
Future studies with larger samples and increased statistical power may allow for more precise differentiation among competing structural models.
Finally, differences between the Chinese and English tasks limit cross-language comparability.
Thus, cross-language patterns may partly reflect measurement methods rather than underlying constructs.
Future studies should use more closely matched tasks across languages.
Together, addressing these limitations will help clarify the developmental, structural, and crosslinguistic mechanisms underlying morpho-lexical integration in bilingual literacy.
This study examined the dimensionality of key cognitive-linguistic skills across proficiency groups in Chinese-English bilingual children.

By testing theoretically motivated models across two proficiency levels, we sought to determine whether these skills function as distinct dimensions or integrate into more general constructs at different levels of bilingual proficiency.
The findings showed that the dimensionality of cognitive-linguistic skills partly varied across languages and proficiency groups.

Whereas L1 Chinese showed a common three-factor structure across proficiency levels, the three-factor structure of L2 English differed between the two groups: phonological and morphological awareness formed a common factor among emerging bilinguals, whereas morphological awareness and vocabulary knowledge formed a morpho-lexical factor among advanced bilinguals.

Together, these findings suggest that morpho-lexical integration may be an important feature of cognitive-linguistic organization whose role may differ across languages and levels of bilingual proficiency, thereby providing a developmental framework for understanding the structure of bilingual literacy.
